Continuous Water Quality Report

Author

Andrew Tran, Vivian Klotz, Lillian McCormick

Introduction

The Department of Water Resources (DWR) and the US Bureau of Reclamation (USBR) are required by Water Right Decision 1641 (D-1641) to collect continuous water chemistry data to monitor the water quality at select sites in the upper San Francisco Estuary (Estuary). This report describes the results of these monitoring efforts for water year 2025 (October 1st 2024 through September 30th 2025) which was classified as above normal in the Sacramento Valley and below normal in the San Joaquin Valley (source).

This report includes mandated stations collected by DWR’s Continuous Environmental Monitoring Program (CEMP) and Suisun Marsh Water Quality Program (SMWQP) as well as USBR’s Delta Water Quality Monitoring Program (USBR). Stations monitored by other programs were not included in this report. Additional information about these programs can be found here.

Methods

Water quality data was continuously monitored at 29 sites throughout the Upper Estuary and were grouped into regions based on their geographic location (Figure 1; Table 1). These sites represent a variety of aquatic habitats, from narrow, freshwater channels to broad, estuarine bays.

Notes:

  • The Sherman Island station (SSI), which was called D22A in previous reports, has been changed back to D11A.

  • The Cache Slough station (C19) is listed as a monitoring station for D-1641 but has not been in operation since 2015 due to lack of use and safety concerns.

Data were collected for six water quality parameters and stations were divided between programs (Table 2). For CEMP and SMWQP, all water samples were collected 1-meter below the water surface using a float-mounted YSI EXO2 multi-parameter water quality sonde. These parameters are:

  • Water Temperature (°C)
  • Specific Conductance (μS/cm 25°C)
  • Dissolved Oxygen (mg/L)
  • pH
  • Turbidity (FNU)
  • Fluorescence (μg/L)

For Reclamation, water samples were collected 1-meter below the water surface using float-mounted Hydrolab MS5 and HL4 water quality sondes. Parameters collected include:

  • Water Temperature (°C)
  • Specific Conductance (μS/cm 25°C)

Regional facet graphs were created for each parameter. The average, minimum, and maximum values were determined for parameter, both overall and per region. Average summary statistics are reported as the mean (μ) ± the standard deviation.

For more in-depth methodology, see here.

Results

Water Temperature

The average water temperature value was 16.80 ± 4.92 °C. Values ranged from 5.90 °C to 28.30 °C. Per region average, minimum, and maximum values are shown in Table 3; time series plots are shown in Figure 2.

Specific Conductance

The average specific conductance value was 3470 ± 5290 µS/cm. Values ranged from 94 µS/cm to 28900 µS/cm. Per region average, minimum, and maximum values are shown in Table 4; time series plots are shown in Figure 3.

Dissolved Oxygen

The average dissolved oxygen value was 8.80 ± 1.30 mg/L. Values ranged from 1.42 mg/L to 14.50 mg/L. Per region average, minimum, and maximum values are shown in Table 5; time series plots are shown in Figure 4.

Stockton Station DO Values

C-EMP monitors DO at the Stockton Ship channel to determine if/when it fall below limits established by the CVRWQCB (1998). For the months that coincide with the passage of fall-run Chinook salmon (October, November, and September), values did not fall below the 6 mg/L limit. For all other months, values did not fall below the 5 mg/L limit. A boxplot of the DO values is shown in Figure 5.

pH

The average pH value was 7.71 ± 0.28. Values ranged from 7.01 to 9.47. Per region average, minimum, and maximum values are shown in Table 6; time series plots are shown in Figure 6.

Turbidity

The average turbidity value was 21.90 ± 20.20 FNU. Values ranged from 0.08 FNU to 215.00 FNU. Per region average, minimum, and maximum values are shown in Table 7; time series plots are shown in Figure 7.

Chlorophyll a Fluorescence

The average fluorescence value was 3.63 ± 4.93 µg/L. Values ranged from 0.28 µg/L to 102.00 µg/L. Per region average, minimum, and maximum values are shown in Table 8; time series plots are shown in Figure 8.

Interpretations

Water Year 2025 was characterized by regional differences in precipitation, with the northern part of the state receiving above average precipitation, and the southern part of the state receiving below average. This was consistent throughout the water year, which resulted in a water year classification of Above Normal. Patterns in water quality generally followed expected seasonal and regional trends. Specific conductivity varied across the stations and throughout the year, depending on Delta outflow and precipitation. The Confluence, Suisun and Grizzly Bays, and Suisun Marsh regions had higher specific conductivity consistent with a dry fall, until larger storms arrived in late December and mid-January. Specific conductivity stayed relatively low until approximately late-May, or late-March in the furthest west station, D6A, which was earlier than in the past water year. Increases in turbidity and decreases in oxygen followed the large storms. Small phytoplankton blooms occurred throughout the year in different regions, including moderate chlorophyll-a fluorescence and higher oxygen in the Suisun and Grizzy Bays in late April and May, and a larger bloom event in the South Delta in July. Dissolved oxygen stayed fairly high throughout the year, with the exception of S33, which showed lower oxygen in late-February to mid-April.

References

[CVRWQCB] Central Valley Regional Water Quality Control Board. (1998). Water Quality Control Plan for the California Regional Water Quality Control Board Central Valley Region, the Sacramento River Basin, and San Joaquin River Basin [Basin Plan] (4th ed.).

[SWRCB] State Water Resources Control Board. (1999). Water Rights Decision 1641 for the Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta and Suisun Marsh (Adopted December 29, 1999, Revised in Accordance with order WR2000-02 March 15, 2000). Sacramento, CA.
